_comment: Checked implications (edges) and ledger facts used by glm_dialogue.py. Every edge names the Lean theorem or ledger claim (RequestProject/GLM/Rule30/claims.csv) that backs it. Premise tags are attached to hypotheses structurally by the puzzle (meta['tags'] or the tagger), never by keywords in the text.

edges.conclusion: white left diagonals never stop: for every D0 there is an eventually white diagonal D >= D0
edges.note: proved for every D0 (Round 39); the refutation of the finite list is consistent with it

edges.conclusion: diagonal D+2 is eventually white iff diagonals D and D+1 are eventually equal
edges.note: the proved form of the white criterion (Round 39)

edges.conclusion: no two consecutive left diagonals are eventually white
the period changes only one step past an eventually white diagonal: it doubles when the outer parity is odd, and is kept when it is even
edges.note: the law the refutation leads to (Round 38)

edges.conclusion: the left-diagonal periods are unbounded iff for every 2^m some eventually white diagonal has an outer neighbour of odd parity
edges.note: To Do 45 is exactly this parity question

edges.conclusion: the left-diagonal periods are unbounded
edges.note: the law locates the doublings; whether infinitely many occur depends on the parities, which are open

edges.conclusion: the centre column reads every left diagonal 20 <= D < 20000 before that diagonal has become periodic
the centre column is not eventually periodic (Problem 1)
edges.note: a family meets the same premises (for every period) while its diagonal read is constant; hypothesis_engine_v10.py states this implication

edges.conclusion: no finite-state observer reading the centre column is eventually always right
no finite automaton reading the binary digits of n computes bit n (so bit n cannot be computed in O(log n))
edges.note: Thue-Morse is aperiodic and computed by a two-state automaton; Problem 1 would not settle Problem 3

edges.conclusion: the statement holds for every index
edges.note: gcd(n^17+9,(n+1)^17+9) = 1 survives every n < 1000 (CERT) and fails at a 52-digit n

edges.conclusion: n^2+n+41 is composite whenever n > 0 and n mod 41 is 0 or 40
41 divides n^2+n+41 iff n mod 41 is 0 or 40
a prime p is a sum of two squares iff p mod 4 is not 3
a prime p is a sum of two squares iff p mod 4 is not 3
distinct Fermat numbers are coprime
distinct Fermat numbers are coprime
J(n) = 2(n - 2^floor(log2 n)) for every n >= 1
the repaired midpoint lo + (hi-lo)/2 is in [lo, hi] for every 16-bit input
the repaired midpoint is always in range
the buggy midpoint leaves [lo, hi] iff lo + hi overflows 16 bits
every n reaches 1
edges.note: only n < 10000 is certified; the general statement is the Collatz conjecture

edges.conclusion: the region count is C(n,4)+C(n,2)+1, not 2^(n-1)
edges.note: the two forms agree for n <= 5 and split at n = 6

edges.conclusion: J(n) = 2(n - 2^floor(log2 n))
every n reaches 1
edges.note: unbounded stopping times are compatible with every n reaching 1 (2^m takes m steps)

edges.conclusion: the period doubles one step past an eventually white diagonal whose inner neighbour has odd parity, and is kept when that parity is even
diagonal D is eventually white iff diagonals D-2 and D-1 are eventually equal

edges.note: if diagonal D-1 is eventually white, diagonals D-3 and D-2 are eventually equal, so their parities agree
the least period is a function of the eventual pattern, so the second conjunct follows from the first

edges.conclusion: the buggy midpoint leaves [lo, hi] iff lo + hi overflows

edges.note: with lo ≤ hi < 2^16, lo + hi ≥ 2^16 forces hi ≥ 2^15, so the second conjunct follows from the first
